metadata.title: Early Foundations of Video Art and CRT Experimentation

content:
Early Foundations of Video Art and CRT Experimentation
Emergence of Consumer Video and Artistic Experimentation
1960s–1970s: As commercial video cameras and portable tape decks (e.g., Sony Portapak) hit the market, artists began using these devices to explore “video” as a raw medium—beyond mere television broadcast.
Nam June Paik is often credited as a pioneer, using television sets with altered circuitry and magnets placed on CRTs to distort images and produce synesthetic, audiovisual pieces.
The Vasulkas: Steina and Woody
Steina (a trained violinist) and Woody (an engineer) Vasulka profoundly influenced the early video art movement. In the late 1960s, they co-founded The Kitchen in New York, a performance and media art space.
They created and modified devices to explore image processing in real time—introducing feedback loops, altering sync signals, and using waveform generators to bend and twist the video raster. Their works often fused abstract patterns with electronic music, forging a new language of audiovisual expression.
CRT Technology Basics
Cathode Ray Tubes rely on an electron beam scanning across a phosphor-coated screen line by line (the “raster”), controlled by deflection coils.
By manipulating the deflection signals or feeding alternative waveforms into the CRT’s circuitry, artists could reshape or warp the final image. This “raster manipulation” laid the groundwork for many analog video synthesizer designs.

Early Video Synthesizers and Image Processors
Rutt/Etra Scan Processor
In the early 1970s, Steve Rutt (an engineer) and Bill Etra (a video artist) developed the Rutt/Etra Scan Processor.
This device allowed users to displace the electron beam in X and Y directions (and sometimes Z for brightness), effectively “sculpting” video into 3D-like waveforms on the screen.
It became famous for its signature rippling “wave” distortions, seen in classic video art pieces and even in some early music videos.
Sandin Image Processor (IP)
Dan Sandin developed the Sandin Image Processor in 1971. It was a patchable, modular video synthesizer enabling real-time colorization, keying, and distortion effects.
Like a modular audio synthesizer, the IP used function generators and signal mixers for creative manipulation of video signals, influencing later systems such as LZX.
Paik-Abe Synthesizer
Co-designed by Nam June Paik and Shuya Abe in 1969, it was another early stand-alone system for colorizing and distorting video inputs.
The device used custom circuitry, making it possible to superimpose and modulate multiple video sources.

Scanimate and Broadcast Motion Graphics
What Was Scanimate?
Scanimate was an analog computer system developed in the late 1960s by the Denver-based company Computer Image Corporation.
It produced those iconic swirling text and lively motion graphics often seen in 1970s TV commercials and station IDs.
Essentially, Scanimate took a video camera feed of artwork or text, then used analog circuits (including deflection and waveform manipulation) to “animate” or morph these images in real time.
Influence on 1970s–1980s Television
Many local stations and ad agencies used Scanimate for vibrant, dynamic titles—a style deeply associated with the disco-era aesthetic.
Digital systems gradually replaced Scanimate in the 1980s and 1990s, but its analog charm remains legendary among motion-graphics aficionados.

Vector Synthesis and Oscilloscope Art
Turning Audio into Imagery
In vector synthesis, signals are sent to the X and Y inputs of an oscilloscope (or a modified CRT display). Instead of a raster sweep, the electron beam is directly steered by audio or control voltages, creating Lissajous curves, abstract shapes, or even more complex patterns.
Artists like Steina Vasulka also played with scanning techniques, using analog computers and custom software to create real-time vector imagery.
Modern Revival
Contemporary artists and instrument designers continue exploring vector synthesis, hooking up modular synth signals to old CRT monitors or scopes. This approach straddles the line between audio oscillator patching and visual generation, marrying sonic and visual forms in real time.

Rise of Video Mixers and Broadcast Gear
Analog Video Mixers
Brands like Panasonic, Videonics, and MX-series mixers offered composite video mixing for live editing, layering, keying, and transitions.
Artists discovered that pushing these mixers beyond their intended design—like overdriving input levels or re-patching outputs back into inputs—could yield glitchy, distorted visuals.
Broadcast Equipment in Art
Time Base Correctors (TBCs), production switchers, and broadcast color correctors became raw materials for artists eager to break the standard broadcast chain.
By repurposing or circuit-bending these devices, new forms of ephemeral, glitch-based art blossomed.

Contemporary Analog Video Synthesis: LZX Industries and Others
LZX Industries
Founded by Lars Larsen (with help from collaborators), LZX Industries builds Eurorack-format modular video synthesis modules.
Inspired by early devices (Sandin IP, Rutt/Etra, etc.), LZX modules let artists patch oscillators, filters, ramps, and keyers to shape composite or component video signals in real time.
Over the past decade, LZX has grown into a cornerstone of the modern hardware video art community, offering increasingly advanced modules that support HD signals, advanced pattern generators, and more.
Other Builders and Platforms
Syntonie (France) offers open-source DIY Eurorack modules for video processing, color encoding/decoding, and glitch effects.
The Vidiot (by Critter & Guitari) and Structure (by Erogenous Tones) are standalone devices bridging analog and digital processing.

Circuit-Bent Video Devices and Glitch Boxes
BPMC (Big Pauper Modified Circuitry)
BPMC is known for customizing mass-market video gear (like older video mixers or consumer FX units) to produce glitchy, chaotic visuals.
They sell “glitch boxes” that disrupt sync signals or color burst circuits, leading to unpredictable meltdown aesthetics.
Tachyons+
Another well-regarded boutique maker of glitch video devices. Tachyons+ modifies vintage hardware or builds from scratch, resulting in unique color smearing, strobing feedback, and digital corruption.
Their gear often finds use in music videos, live visual performances, and experimental film.
LoFi Future
LoFi Future similarly custom-modifies video mixers, internal circuits, and external controllers to achieve real-time glitch manipulations.
Encourages a DIY ethic—many practitioners exchange tips and schematics for personal customization.

The Radiator Laser Synth and Hybrid Approaches
The Radiator Laser Synth fuses laser projection and analog wave synthesis: control voltages or audio signals drive laser galvos, producing fluid, evolving light patterns in physical space.
This approach expands “video synthesis” beyond CRTs to involve lasers, projectors, LED walls, or other visual output devices that can respond to analog waveforms.
Artists often combine these methods with camera feedback loops, layering multiple mediums to create immersive environments.

Broader Cultural Impact and Ongoing Traditions
Live Visual Performances (VJ Culture)
Analog gear remains a beloved corner of the VJ community. Even with digital software available, many performers prize the warm unpredictability and hands-on approach of hardware.
Live camera feeds can be routed through hardware mixers and glitch boxes, re-projected or displayed on vintage CRTs for immersive events.
DIY and Open-Source
A large contingent of video artists build or hack their own devices, circulating schematics online, hosting workshops, and publishing open-source firmware.
Communities on platforms like YouTube, GitHub, and video art forums share knowledge about reversing obsolete broadcast gear or designing new analog circuits.
Exhibitions and Archives
Institutions like the Vasulka Chamber (in Reykjavik, Iceland) archive works and documentation from the Vasulkas, preserving the lineage of video art experimentation.
Galleries and new media festivals increasingly highlight historical analog equipment as cultural artifacts, demonstrating how these clunky but ingenious machines shaped the language of video art.

Reflecting on the Continuing Analog Renaissance
Despite the ubiquity of digital editing software, the tactile immediacy and distinctive look of analog video remain compelling.
Modern companies (LZX, Syntonie, BPMC, Tachyons+, LoFi Future) keep the flame alive, pushing the aesthetics of glitch and synthesis into fresh territory—often blending analog circuitry with digital processing or advanced lighting setups.
The line between “broadcast equipment” and “creative instrument” keeps blurring. Artists no longer shy away from reengineering or breaking “professional gear” if it offers new creative frontiers.
From the pioneering days of the Vasulkas and Rutt/Etra to the boutique glitch boxes and modular rigs of today, analog video art persists as an evolving medium—breathing new life into decades-old CRT technology and forging new sonic-visual worlds that continue to surprise, challenge, and inspire. If you’d like to take a deeper plunge into any specific sub-topic—be it the technicalities of vector scanning, the internal workings of a Scanimate, or the design philosophies behind LZX modules—just say the word.
